atlas-is.0061: ENIC/NARIC Iceland sits at the University of Iceland; for regulated jobs the profession’s own authority decides, such as the Directorate of Health for medical staff and the Ministry of Industries and Innovation for technical services and design. For other jobs Work in Iceland and EURES advise bringing diplomas, translated into English or Icelandic. We did not find fees or timelines.
atlas-is.0062: The University of Iceland and Reykjavík University are where employers go to recruit (61 organisations at Reykjavík University’s Career Days in 2026, Tengslatorg at the University of Iceland); we found no ranking of schools in hiring beyond those two.
atlas-is.0063: We found no dual-study track for graduate jobs; the nearest things are internships posted through Tengslatorg, summer research jobs, and Arion’s 15-month graduate programme. The IÐAN educational centre handles vocational education and recognition, a separate trades route.
atlas-is.0064: Public administration, education, health and social work employed 77,246 of 234,604 people (32.9%) in June 2026; the section includes some private providers, and state jobs on Starfatorg are mostly in Icelandic.
atlas-is.0065: A non-EEA hire needs an expert permit: the employer must show it tried to hire an Icelander or an EEA, EFTA or Faroese national first, and a trade union must confirm the terms follow the collective agreement. CCP’s careers page says it has experience relocating people from around the world; we found no count of employers who sponsor. The rules are on the Visas page.
atlas-is.0066: VR, the trade union, says a photo is customary in Iceland though generally not done overseas: place it in the upper left or right corner beside your name and keep it conventional.
atlas-is.0067: VR advises a CV of about 1–2 A4 pages, in reverse chronological order for the last 10–15 years, education first if you have just graduated; personal details such as marital status or number of children are left out.
atlas-is.0068: VR calls the cover letter especially useful for jobs that need specialised knowledge and asks for half a page to one page; EURES says a concise CV and cover letter matter most, and many companies use electronic forms that let you attach both.
atlas-is.0069: VR advises giving 2–3 referees (former employers, teachers, co-workers) with name, workplace, title and phone number, asking their permission first; written references are rarely used. We did not find when employers call them.
atlas-is.0070: EURES recommends bringing your diplomas and certificates, translated into English or Icelandic; certified copies of diplomas are asked for in an expert work-permit application, not in ordinary applications.
atlas-is.0071: VR lists “wage expectations” among the questions to expect at the interview, not in the CV or letter; Icelandic contracts state the salary before tax, which Work in Iceland says can leave a foreign hire unsure of take-home pay.
atlas-is.0072: We found no page on background checks in Icelandic graduate hiring; referees are phoned (VR), and a foreign hire’s former employer’s reference is recommended with a permit application.
atlas-is.0073: In a country of about 400,000 people, personal contact is the main channel.
atlas-is.0074: EURES tells jobseekers to let their contacts know they are looking, and Work in Iceland says to contact firms and recruiters directly.
atlas-is.0075: English-language roles can be applied for from abroad: CCP’s process is a phone call and video interviews, and EURES jobs must have an English version. EEA citizens need no permit; others cannot start work before the residence and work permits are granted.
atlas-is.0076: Most vacancies are in Icelandic; roles suited to non-speakers are advertised in English or in both languages, and Alfreð can filter listings by language requirement. Icelandic is an important advantage.
atlas-is.0077: CCP’s process, the one tech process we could read, is a human-reviewed application, a short phone call, a video interview that may include a skills test or an SHL psychometric assessment, a third interview on results or technical points, and sometimes an onsite day, aimed at six weeks.
atlas-is.0078: VR lists the questions to prepare: why you applied, why you left your last job, a time you worked with colleagues, how you handle time pressure and your wage expectations; Career Days in January include micro interviews, with no registration, at 22 companies.
atlas-is.0079: We found no page on assessment centres, dress or the time from application to offer for Icelandic graduate jobs.
atlas-is.0080: A written contract is required if you are hired for more than one month and work more than 8 hours a week, signed within 2 months of starting; it must follow the collective agreement, and terms that fall below it are invalid.
atlas-is.0081: Trial periods and notice depend on the union agreement: the LIV (retail and office) agreement gives a 3-month trial with 1 week’s notice, then 1 month from 3 to 6 months and 3 months after 6 months; SGS gives 12 days after 2 weeks, 1 month after 3 months and 3 months after 3 years.
atlas-is.0082: Paid holiday is at least 24 working days a year and holiday pay is at least 10.17% of wages; contracts quote salary before tax. We did not read a page on December or holiday bonuses, on whether graduates negotiate, or on how long employers give you to decide.
atlas-is.0083: For a non-EEA hire the employer applies with a signed contract, a union confirmation that terms match the collective agreements, and proof it tried to hire an Icelandic, EEA, EFTA or Faroese national first; certified diplomas are needed, and work experience of about seven years generally counts as equal to a university degree.
atlas-is.0084: The worker cannot start before the residence and work permits are granted. A tax discount taxes 75% of income for the first three years if you apply within three months of starting work.
atlas-is.0085: Raise it early and in English-language roles, where employers are used to it: CCP says it has relocated people from around the world, while an employer who advertises only in Icelandic is unlikely to be set up for it.
atlas-is.0086: Portals named by Work in Iceland: Alfreð (mostly Icelandic, some English), Job.is, Störf (Icelandic and English), Tvinna (design, computing and data roles, Icelandic and English), Northstack (start-up news with occasional job posts, English), Starfatorg (public sector), Reykjavík city’s jobs page, Vinnumálastofnun and EURES.
atlas-is.0087: Agencies: Brú Talent, Hagvangur, HH ráðgjöf, Intellecta and Ráðum. For students, Tengslatorg at the University of Iceland and Reykjavík University’s Career Days in January; the Arion graduate programme page and CCP’s careers page for named employers.
atlas-is.0088: Alfreð’s filters cover job type (full-time, summer, internship, temporary and others) and language requirement, and its talent pool surfaces unadvertised jobs.
atlas-is.0089: Waiting for an advertisement: Work in Iceland’s advice is to find the firms that match your skills and contact them directly, since agencies fill unadvertised roles.
atlas-is.0090: Missing the January window: Career Days, the Student Innovation Fund (to 17 February) and Arion’s graduate round all fall in the first weeks of the year.
atlas-is.0091: Searching only English listings and concluding there is nothing: most local vacancies are in Icelandic, so use the portals’ language filters, and read EURES for English versions.
atlas-is.0092: Promising a start date before the permit: a non-EEA hire cannot begin work until the residence and work permits are granted.
atlas-is.0093: Banks advertise and hire in Icelandic; Arion’s graduate programme page is in English but does not say what language level it asks for.
atlas-is.0094: CCP says English is the common language across its studios, applications are made in English and at least one interview is in English; Tvinna and Störf carry computing roles in Icelandic and English.
atlas-is.0095: Starfatorg, the state job site, is mostly in Icelandic; the exception we read is the EFTA, ESA and FMO Junior Professional Programme, presented in English.
atlas-is.0096: No national figure for how many interns or trainees are kept; Arion publishes no placement rate for its graduate programme.
atlas-is.0097: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa or residence permit and are treated as Icelanders.
atlas-is.0098: Staying over three months, register your right of residence and address with Registers Iceland (forms A-260 and A-270) to get your ID number (kennitala); it is free.
atlas-is.0099: Bring an S1 form for health cover from arrival; the address must be a proper residential property.
atlas-is.0100: Full-time study at a recognised Icelandic university; apply to the Directorate of Immigration (ÚTL) by 1 June for autumn or 1 October for spring.
atlas-is.0101: Since 8 July 2026 students may work up to 60% of full time in term and full time in holidays without a separate work permit, but not before the card is issued and never self-employed.
atlas-is.0102: Renewal needs 75% of the year’s credits. Iceland does not apply the EU student-mobility rules, so exchange students from another EU country need their own permit.
atlas-is.0108: Only for an internship that is a compulsory part of a degree you are studying abroad, with a training agreement and funds; internships after graduating or purely commercial ones are not allowed.
atlas-is.0110: Job-search permit after an Icelandic degree
